CASE STUDIES

Kondapalli Reserve Forest (Andhra Pradesh)
Linking LULC Change to Natural Resource Accounting

Why LULC Matters for NRA
•LULC = spatial representation of natural capital stocks.
•Temporal LULC maps → show depletion, additions, or 
transformation of resources.
•Urbanization is a key driver of:
• Forest/agriculture → Built-up.
• Decline in ecosystem services.
•Basis for land accounts in SEEA 
(System of Environmental-Economic Accounting).

Stocks & Flows Framework
• • Natural capital stock = forest, agriculture, water
• • Manufactured capital stock = built-up area
• • Flow = Change in stock between time periods
• Forest ↓ → loss of carbon sequestration, biodiversity, 
water regulation
• • Forest 1990–2015: -9.74 km² → negative flow
• • Built-up 1990–2017: +59.16 km² → positive flow of 
manufactured capital
• Built-up ↑ → gain in infrastructure, but ↑ waste & 
emissions
• • Accounts: Translate physical flows → monetary 
accounts (e.g., carbon, provisioning services)

Worked Example: Carbon Valuation
• Forest loss (1990–2015) = 9.74 km² = 974 ha
• Assume mean biomass = 30 tC/ha
• Total C loss = 974 × 30 = 29,220 tC
• Convert to CO₂ = 29,220 × 3.67 = 107,140 tCO₂
• Value (Carbon price scenarios):
• • At US$5/tCO₂:107,140 × 5 = US$535,700 
US$10/tCO₂:107,140 × 10 = US$1,071,400 
US$20/tCO₂:107,140 × 20 = US$2,142,800

NRA links ecosystem changes to economic valuation

1988–2022:
• Water bodies: 
stable (67.9 → 65.7 km²).
• Vegetation: 
sharp decline (220.7 → 139.8 km²).
• Agriculture/fallow: 
reduced from 84.8 → 15.7 km².
• Built-up: 
major increase (15.6 → 167.8 km²)
Economic Impact:
Loss of agricultural productivity, 
increased water stress, livelihood 
shifts.

1988–2023: • Water bodies: 442.1 → 347.7 km² (−94.4 km²).
Vegetation: 767.3 → 650.3 km². • Pokkali fields: 97.1 → 57.7 km².
Built-up: 80.8 → 340.6 km².
Economic Impact: Decline in fisheries (fish landings halved since 2000), 
loss of Pokkali-rice-practice, tourism pressure.

Economic Accounting Implications
• Loss of fishery resources = reduced income for local communities.
• Agricultural decline = food insecurity, job losses.
• Urban growth = external costs (pollution, flooding).
• Declining water storage = higher disaster costs (floods, water crisis).
• Ecosystem degradation = reduced tourism potential.
Key Findings:
• 20–40% vegetation decline.
• Built-up increased 3–4x.
• Water bodies reduced by ~100 km² in Vembanad.
• Traditional Pokkali rice farming reduced 40%.
Accounting Framework:
• Direct use values (fisheries, agriculture).
• Indirect use values (flood regulation, water purification).
• Non-use values (biodiversity, cultural heritage).
